title: Understanding herbal safety
subtitle: A foundations reading on herb-drug interactions, contraindications, and when to see a doctor rather than reach for a herb
excerpt: This reading explains the four safety categories used across the herbal-medicine category, drug interactions, pharmacological effects at dose, cumulative toxicity, and look-alike risk, and gives the framework for using safety flags. It covers the most important interaction classes, the difference between traditional caution and evidence-based contraindication, and the clear lines where herbal self-care stops and medical advice is necessary.
sourceNotes: Original Homemade editorial. Safety frameworks reference: EMA HMPC guidelines on herbal medicinal products; WHO guidelines on safety monitoring of herbal medicines (2004); Brinker F., Herb Contraindications and Drug Interactions (2010), general safety classes.

glossaryTerms.definition: A reason to avoid using a herb or preparation entirely, rather than to use it with caution. Absolute contraindications (pregnancy with emmenagogues, pyrrolizidine alkaloid herbs) mean: do not use. Relative contraindications mean: use only under professional supervision.

An herb-drug interaction mediated by the liver's cytochrome P450 enzyme system, which processes most prescription drugs. Herbs that induce CYP450 enzymes (like St John's wort) reduce drug blood levels; herbs that inhibit them (like some flavonoids) can raise drug levels to potentially toxic concentrations.

content.text: Herbs are medicinally active. The same properties that make a herb useful can also cause harm. These include alkaloids, tannins, aromatic oils, and glycosides. Harm occurs when they are misused, combined with the wrong medication, or taken by people with specific conditions. The safety flags in this category organise these risks into four practical classes.
The main herb safety risk is the interaction with prescription medication. The most important pathway is the

system. St John's wort is the key example: it speeds up the liver's processing of dozens of drugs, lowering their blood levels. Affected drugs include the contraceptive pill, organ-rejection drugs, HIV drugs, and warfarin. This one herb accounts for more recorded drug interactions than any other in herbal medicine.

Rule: tell your pharmacist or prescriber before adding any herb to prescribed medication. The main groups to flag: blood thinners and heart drugs. Also: antidepressants, epilepsy drugs, organ-rejection drugs, hormonal contraceptives, and HIV drugs. Name the specific drug rather than the category.

Some herbs have measurable medicinal effects that become risks at high dose or in specific groups. Licorice root at high dose or long-term use causes salt retention, potassium loss, and raised blood pressure. This is a real risk for people with high blood pressure or kidney disease, but not a problem in healthy people at low doses for a short course. Uterine stimulants (mugwort, yarrow at medicinal dose, pennyroyal) stimulate the uterus and are not safe in pregnancy, though they are used for their traditional purposes otherwise. Sedating herbs (valerian, hops) increase the effect of alcohol and prescribed sedatives. The safety flag in each entry names the specific group or situation where the risk applies.

A small number of herbs are safe for short courses but accumulate problematic compounds with extended use. Comfrey root contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids (PAs) that are harmful to the liver and cancer-linked with sustained internal use, the same herb is safe externally for short-course wound treatment. Coltsfoot and borage also contain PAs. Thujone-containing plants (sage, mugwort, wormwood) are safe at culinary doses but problematic at high medicinal doses or for long periods. The short-course-only flags in this category exist for exactly this reason.

Wild plant foraging carries a risk that shop-bought dried herbs do not: misidentification. The main UK pairs to know: yarrow and hemlock, elder berries and dwarf elder (toxic berries), wild garlic leaf and lily of the valley. The look-alike-risk flag appears on foraging entries only. If you are unsure of a plant, do not use it.
When to see a doctor rather than use a herb

Herbal self-care is right for mild, familiar, short-term conditions in healthy adults: a cold, minor digestive upset, tension headache, dry cough, or mild insomnia. It is not right for symptoms that are new, severe, worsening, or unexplained. Not for conditions that need medical management. Not for warning signs: chest pain, unexplained weight loss, nerve symptoms, or blood in stool or urine. The when-not-to-use section of each entry lists these cut-off points. They are navigation, not disclaimers.
Traditional caution versus evidence-based reason to avoid

in this category come in two kinds. First: evidence-based ones with documented risk. St John's wort with the contraceptive pill. Comfrey root taken internally. Licorice root with high blood pressure. Second: traditional cautions based on a lack of safety data, not proven harm. This includes most herbs in pregnancy and in infants. No reported harm is not the same as proven safe.
